claim: Signed and unsigned reward prediction errors (RPEs) contribute to learning by modulating a dynamically changing learning rate.
source: By fitting reinforcement learning models to behavior, we find that both RPEs contribute to learning by modulating a dynamically changing learning rate.
evidence: Supported by computational modeling of behavioral data showing that models including both signed and unsigned RPE modulation of learning rate fit better than models without these components.

claim: Both signed and unsigned RPEs enhance memory.
source: We further characterize the effects of these RPE signals on memory and show that both signed and unsigned RPEs enhance memory, in line with midbrain dopamine and locus-coeruleus modulation of hippocampal plasticity, thereby reconciling separate findings in the literature.
evidence: Supported by mixed-effects modeling and Bayesian hierarchical modeling showing memory enhancement effects of both RPE types.

claim: Dopaminergic RPE increases dopamine release when rewards are better than expected and decreases its release when rewards are worse than expected.
source: This signal modulates dopaminergic firing from the midbrain, increasing dopamine release when rewards are better than expected, and decreasing its release when rewards are worse than expected ('signed RPE'; Barto, 1995; Montague et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature on dopaminergic signaling.

claim: The dopaminergic RPE transfers from unpredictable reward outcome to the cue predicting the reward over the course of learning.
source: Over the course of learning, this dopaminergic RPE transfers from unpredictable reward outcome to the cue predicting the reward (Schultz et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citation to established literature on dopaminergic signaling dynamics.

claim: Neural plasticity in the hippocampus is modulated by dopamine.
source: This signed RPE could also give rise to stronger memory traces, given that neural plasticity in the hippocampus – the key structure for episodic memory – is modulated by dopamine (Lisman and Grace, 2005; Shohamy and Adcock, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on dopaminergic modulation of hippocampal plasticity.

claim: The Pearce-Hall model posits that attention is enhanced for cues that co-occur with large unsigned RPEs.
source: In fact, the Pearce-Hall model of learning (Pearce and Hall, 1980), which contradicts the Mackintosh model, posits that attention is enhanced for cues that are accompanied by surprise, that is, those that co-occur with large unsigned RPEs.
evidence: Supported by citation to the Pearce-Hall model of learning.

claim: The locus coeruleus-norepinephrine system responds to unexpected changes in stimulus-reinforcement contingencies, regardless of the sign of the outcome.
source: The effects of unsigned RPEs are thought to be mediated by the locus coeruleus-norepinephrine system, which responds to unexpected changes in stimulus-reinforcement contingencies, regardless of the sign of the outcome (for a review, see Sara, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to review literature on the locus coeruleus-norepinephrine system.

claim: The locus coeruleus co-releases dopamine with norepinephrine, providing an alternative source of dopamine to the hippocampus.
source: Moreover, recent evidence points to the locus coeruleus (LC), which co-releases dopamine with norpeinephrine, as providing an alternative source of dopamine to the hippocampus, giving rise to hippocampal memories (Kempadoo et al., 2016; Takeuchi et al., 2016; Wagatsuma et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to recent literature on locus coeruleus function.

claim: Unsigned, but not signed, RPEs experienced at reward outcome boost learning and memory.
source: Previously, we found that unsigned, but not signed, RPEs experienced at reward outcome boost learning and memory (Rouhani et al., 2018), consistent with work showing better memory for surprising events (Greve et al., 2017; Antony et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work by the authors and related literature.

claim: Signed RPEs experienced at reward-predictive cue enhance memory.
source: There is also recent support for signed RPEs experienced at reward-predictive cue to enhance memory (Jang et al., 2019), reminiscent of work showing memory benefits during periods of high-reward anticipation (Adcock et al., 2006; Murty and Adcock, 2014; Stanek et al., 2019; Wittmann et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to recent literature on memory enhancement during reward anticipation.

claim: Unsigned RPE at reward outcome boosted learning rate in both Experiment 1 and Experiment 2.
source: We found the unsigned RPE at reward outcome boosted learning rate in both experiments, thereby providing direct behavioral evidence for this 'Pearce-Hall' component on learning rate (mixed-effects linear regression, Experiment 1: β = 0.10, t = 6.39, p<0.001; Experiment 2: β = 0.07 t=8.79, p<0.001; see Figure 2—figure supplement 1 for empirical learning rates).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data from both experiments.

claim: Signed cue RPE was anti-correlated with learning rate.
source: We found that a signed cue RPE was anti-correlated with learning rate, potentially demonstrating stronger associative links and more stable values for more valuable cues (β = −0.02 t = −2.31, p=0.02).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: The cue RPE modulation of learning rate was not merely due to the greater learned separation between the two cue values, but specific to more stable updating for the high-valued cues.
source: Critically, we found this effect even when controlling for any effect of the unsigned cue RPE on learning rate (which was not itself significant, β = −0.01 t = −1.35, p=0.18). This suggests that the cue RPE modulation of learning rate was not merely due to the greater learned separation between the two cue values, but specific to more stable updating for the high-valued cues.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis controlling for confounding variables.

claim: Participants separated the values of two scene categories more in the 20¢−80¢ condition than in the 40¢−60¢ condition.
source: As expected, participants separated the values of two scene categories more in the 20¢−80¢ condition than in the 40¢−60¢ condition (Figure 2B), both in general and as a function of trial number during learning (mixed-effects linear regression, value separation as a function of learning condition: β = 18.62, t = 25.87, p<0.001; interaction between learning condition and trial number: β = 5.40, t = 13.64, p<0.001).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data and reference to figure.

claim: Participants learned better and were more accurate in the instructed memory version compared to the incidental memory version.
source: Although the instructions regarding value learning and prediction were identical for all participants, we did find overall differences in learning across the two memory-instruction conditions. Participants learned better and were more accurate in the instructed memory version: their estimates were closer to the actual underlying means of the scene categories and those estimates became more accurate over time (learning accuracy as a function of instructed-incidental memory: β = 4.35, t = 8.16, p<0.001; interaction between instructed-incidental memory and trial number: β = 0.48, t = 2.08, p=0.04).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data comparing the two memory instruction conditions.

claim: Participants' estimates were, on average, lower during the pandemic than before, demonstrating more pessimistic expectations overall.
source: Interestingly, participants' estimates, and thus expectations for reward, were, on average, lower during the pandemic than before, demonstrating more pessimistic expectations overall (β = −1.17, t = −2.65, p=0.008).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis comparing data collected during different time periods.

claim: The RW-PH-M-D model (including Pearce-Hall, Mackintosh, and decay components) predicted participant value estimates best in Experiment 2.
source: The model that included all three tested modulators of learning rate—an unsigned RPE at outcome (Pearce-Hall component), a signed RPE at cue (Mackintosh component), and an exponential decay—predicted participant value estimates best (Figure 2B,C,E, Table 1).
evidence: Supported by model comparison using likelihood-ratio tests.

claim: In the high-variance condition, there was a lower average memory score for cue events and a higher average memory score for outcome events, compared to the low-variance condition.
source: We found an interaction of cue versus outcome memory by variance condition, such that in the high-variance condition, there was a lower average memory score for cue events, and a higher average memory score for outcome events, compared to the low-variance condition (μ high-variance cue memory = 6.44, μ low-variance cue memory = 6.57, μ high-variance outcome memory = 5.79, μ low-variance outcome memory = 5.54; mixed-effects linear regression: β = −0.37, t = −2.78, p=0.005).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of memory data across variance conditions.

claim: There was a significant difference in memory for outcome events between high and low variance conditions.
source: Within the interaction, there was a significant difference in memory for outcome events (β = −0.25, t = −2.09, p=0.04) but not for cue events (β = 0.12, t = 1.41, p=0.16).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of memory data.

claim: In Experiment 1, cue memory did not change relative to outcome memory throughout learning.
source: In line with our predictions, in Experiment 1, we did not find cue memory to change relative to outcome memory throughout learning (mixed-effects linear regression, memory as a function of the interaction between event type (cue or outcome) and learning trial, β = 0.009, t = 0.13, p=0.90; Figure 3A)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of memory data and reference to figure.

claim: In Experiment 2, memory for cue events improved throughout the experiment, relative to memory for outcome events, in both difficulty conditions.
source: whereas in Experiment 2, memory for cue events improved throughout the experiment, relative to memory for outcome events, in both difficulty conditions (interaction between event type and learning trial, 40¢−60¢ condition: β = −0.24, t = −3.76, p<0.001; 20¢−80¢ condition: β = −0.20, t = −3.29, p<0.001; Figure 3B–C).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of memory data and reference to figures.

claim: The increase in cue memory as a function of learning was not found in the 40¢−60¢ learning condition of the incidental memory version.
source: We did not find the increase in cue memory as a function of learning in the 40¢−60¢ learning condition (interaction between event type and learning trial: β = 0.07, t = 1.11, p=0.27; three-way interaction between event type, instructed-incidental memory and learning trial β = 0.31, t = 3.39, p<0.001; Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of memory data and reference to figure.

claim: The increase in cue memory was replicated in the 20¢−80¢ condition of the incidental memory version.
source: However, we did replicate the increase in cue memory in the 20¢−80¢ condition (interaction between event type and learning trial: β = −0.17, t = −2.79, p=0.005; three-way interaction between event type, instructed-incidental memory and learning trial: β = 0.04, t = 0.41, p=0.68; Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of memory data and reference to figure.

claim: Better individual learning predicted a greater increase in memory for cue events but not for outcome events.
source: Overall, better individual learning predicted a greater increase in memory for cue events (linear regression: β = 0.02, t = 3.07, p=0.002), but not for outcome events (β = 0.001, t = 0.24, p=0.81; interaction between event type and learning performance: β = −0.01, t = −2.29, p=0.02).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of individual differences in learning and memory.

claim: The relationship between learning performance and increase in cue memory was stronger in the incidental memory task than in the instructed one.
source: This relationship was stronger in the incidental memory task (β = 0.02, t = 3.61, p<0.001; see Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) than in the instructed one (β = −0.004, t = −0.61, p=0.55, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A; interaction between instructed-incidental memory and learning performance: β = 0.03, t = 2.61, p=0.009)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis comparing the two memory instruction conditions.

claim: Unsigned outcome RPEs enhanced memory for outcome images in all experiments.
source: In all experiments, we found that unsigned outcome RPEs enhanced memory for outcome images (outcome memory as a function of |outcome RPE|, Experiment 1: M = 0.14, HDI [0.06, 0.23], β = 0.19, t = 3.51, p<0.001, Figure 4A; Experiment 2 - instructed memory: M = 0.14, HDI [0.05, 0.23], β = 0.09, t = 2.59, p=0.009, Figure 4D; Experiment 2 - incidental memory: M = 0.13, HDI [0.06, 0.19], β = 0.11, t = 3.01, p=0.003, Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by Bayesian hierarchical modeling and mixed-effects regression across all experiments.

claim: Unsigned outcome RPEs due to reward variance and change points separately increased memory for outcome images in Experiment 1.
source: We found separate effects of RPEs due only to reward variance and those due to change points on increasing memory for outcome images (outcome memory as a function of variance RPEs: β = 0.14, t = 2.38, p=0.02; outcome memory as a function of change-point RPEs: β = 0.24, t = 2.08, p=0.04).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis separating different sources of unsigned RPEs.

claim: In Experiment 1, unsigned outcome RPEs boosted memory for cue images from that same trial, with a median parameter estimate half the size of that for outcome images.
source: In Experiment 1, we also found unsigned outcome RPEs to boost memory for cue images from that same trial, but with a median parameter estimate half the size of that for outcome images (cue memory as a function of |outcome RPE|: M = 0.08, HDI [−0.01, 0.16], β = 0.10, t = 2.29, p=0.02, Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by Bayesian hierarchical modeling and mixed-effects regression.

claim: In Experiment 2, unsigned outcome RPE enhanced memory only for outcome images, not for cue images.
source: We did not find this effect in any of the conditions of Experiment 2, where unsigned outcome RPE enhanced memory only for outcome images (Experiment 2 - instructed memory, cue memory as a function of |outcome RPE|: M = −0.02, HDI [−0.11, 0.06], β = −0.01, t = −0.46, p=0.64, interaction between event type (cue or outcome event) and |outcome RPE|: β = 0.09, t = 2.06, p=0.04; Experiment 2 - incidental memory, cue memory as a function of |outcome RPE|: M = −0.004, HDI [−0.07, 0.07], β = 0.006, t = 0.20, p=0.84, interaction between event type and |outcome RPE|: β = 0.09, t = 1.98, p=0.05, Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by Bayesian hierarchical modeling and mixed-effects regression.

claim: Signed outcome RPEs did not influence memory for cue or outcome images in either experiment.
source: As expected based on previous work (Rouhani et al., 2018), we did not find any influence of signed outcome RPEs on memory for cue or outcome images in either experiment (Figure 4B,F; cue memory as a function of signed outcome RPE, Experiment 1: M = −0.02, HDI [−0.11, 0.06], β = −0.05, t = −1.04, p=0.30; Experiment 2 - instructed memory, M = 0.002, HDI [−0.07, 0.07], β = −0.02, t = −0.66, p=0.51; Experiment 2 - incidental memory, M = −0.01, HDI [−0.08, 0.05], β = −0.003, t = −0.08, p=0.93; outcome memory as a function of signed outcome RPE, Experiment 1: M = −0.0007, HDI [−0.09, 0.08], β = −0.004, t = −0.07, p=0.95; Experiment 2 - instructed memory, M = −0.03, HDI [−0.10, 0.03], β = −0.05, t = −1.46, p=0.15; Experiment 2 - incidental memory, M = −0.05, HDI [−0.11, 0.02], β = −0.06, t = −1.61, p=0.11).
evidence: Supported by Bayesian hierarchical modeling and mixed-effects regression across experiments, and citation to prior work.

claim: In the instructed memory version of Experiment 2, signed cue RPEs boosted memory for both cue and outcome events.
source: In the instructed memory version of Experiment 2, we found that signed cue RPEs (i.e. the signed difference between the participant-reported value of the current cue and the most-recently reported value of the alternative cue) boosted memory for both cue and outcome events, such that memory of higher (relative) value scenes was better than that for lower (relative) value scenes (cue memory as a function of signed cue RPE: M = 0.08, HDI [0.01, 0.15], β = 0.08, t = 2.64, p=0.008; outcome memory as a function of signed cue RPE: M = 0.06, HDI [−0.01, 0.12], β = 0.07, t = 2.23, p=0.03; Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by Bayesian hierarchical modeling and mixed-effects regression.

claim: In the incidental memory version of Experiment 2, signed cue RPE enhanced memory for cue images but not outcome images.
source: In the incidental version, we replicated the effect of cue RPE on memory for cue images, but not on memory for outcome images (cue memory as a function of signed cue RPE: M = 0.10, HDI [0.04, 0.17], β = 0.09, t = 3.04, p=0.002; outcome memory as a function of signed cue RPE: M = 0.03, HDI [−0.04, 0.09], β = 0.03, t = 0.80, p=0.42; Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by Bayesian hierarchical modeling and mixed-effects regression.

claim: Unsigned cue RPE enhanced overall memory in the instructed memory version of Experiment 2.
source: We found a separate effect of unsigned cue RPE on memory, such that the more participants had separated the values of the two scene categories (i.e. the more they had learned), the better their memory for scene images. This effect was evident in overall memory in the instructed memory version of Experiment 2 (memory as a function of |cue RPE|: β = 0.07, t = 2.49, p=0.01)
evidence: Supported by mixed-effects regression analysis.

claim: In the instructed memory version of Experiment 2, the effects of unsigned cue RPE on cue and outcome memory separately were only trending to significance.
source: however, when quantifying the effect for cue and outcome memory separately, each of them was only trending to significance (cue memory as a function of |cue RPE|: M = 0.09, HDI [0.01, 0.16], β = 0.07, t = 1.88, p=0.06; outcome memory as a function of |cue RPE|: M = 0.06, HDI [−0.01, 0.13], β = 0.08, t = 1.82, p=0.07; Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by Bayesian hierarchical modeling and mixed-effects regression.

claim: In the incidental memory version of Experiment 2, unsigned cue RPEs significantly increased memory for cue images but not outcome images.
source: In the incidental version of Experiment 2, unsigned cue RPEs significantly increased memory for cue images (cue memory as a function of |cue RPE|: M = 0.12, HDI [0.05, 0.18], β = 0.10, t = 2.93, p=0.003), but not outcome images (outcome memory as a function of |cue RPE|: M = 0.02, HDI [−0.05, 0.08], β = 0.01, t = 0.30, p=0.76; interaction between event type and |cue RPE|: β = −0.10, t = −2.22, p=0.03; Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by Bayesian hierarchical modeling and mixed-effects regression.

claim: Reward outcome did not predict memory in any of the experiments.
source: We did not find reward outcome, in of itself or in an interaction with cue or outcome event, to predict memory in any of the experiments (memory as a function of reward outcome, Experiment 1: β = −0.03, t = −0.68, p=0.50, interaction between event type and reward outcome: β = 0.07, t = 1.07, p=0.29; Experiment 2 - instructed memory: β = 0.03, t = 0.91, p=0.36, interaction between event type and reward outcome: β = 0.02, t = 0.55, p=0.58; Experiment 2 - incidental memory: β = 0.05, t = 1.51, p=0.13, interaction between event type and reward outcome: β = −0.04, t = −0.98, p=0.33).
evidence: Supported by mixed-effects regression analysis across all experiments.

claim: Participant value estimates did not predict memory in Experiment 1.
source: When testing the effect of participant value estimates on memory, we similarly did not find participant value estimates, in of themselves or in an interaction with cue or outcome event, to predict memory in Experiment 1 (memory as a function of value estimate, β = −0.007, t = −0.15, p=0.88, interaction between event type and value estimate: β = −0.004, t = −0.06, p=0.95).
evidence: Supported by mixed-effects regression analysis.

claim: In Experiment 2, value estimates were strongly correlated with the signed RPE at cue.
source: In Experiment 2, the value estimates were strongly correlated with the signed RPE at cue (r > 0.80), therefore we could not enter them into a single model.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis.

claim: In the instructed memory version of Experiment 2, value estimates were trending in enhancing memory.
source: When tested alone, value estimates were trending in enhancing memory in the instructed memory version of Experiment 2 (memory as a function of value estimate, β = 0.06, t = 1.89, p=0.06, interaction between event type and value estimate: β = 0.05, t = 1.19, p=0.24)
evidence: Supported by mixed-effects regression analysis.

claim: In the incidental memory version of Experiment 2, value estimates enhanced memory.
source: and enhanced memory in the incidental memory version (memory as a function of value estimate, β = 0.08, t = 2.58, p=0.01, interaction between event type and value estimate: β = −0.03, t = −0.62, p=0.53).
evidence: Supported by mixed-effects regression analysis.

claim: The mnemonic modulation by value estimates is attributable to prediction errors rather than value estimates alone.
source: However, given that value estimates did not influence memory when there was no prediction error at cue (Experiment 1), we believe the parsimonious interpretation is that this mnemonic modulation is attributable to prediction errors rather than value estimates alone.
evidence: Based on inference from comparing results across experiments.

claim: In the instructed memory version of Experiment 2, participants preferred both cues and outcomes associated with higher rewards.
source: As expected, in the instructed memory version, participants preferred both cues and outcomes associated with higher rewards (mixed-effects logistic regression, choice as a function of reward difference: β = 1.59, z = 20.13, p<0.001; Figure 5A)
evidence: Supported by logistic regression analysis of choice data.

claim: In the instructed memory version of Experiment 2, participants preferred images for which they had reported higher subjective value when controlling for the effect of reward outcome on choice.
source: and preferred images for which they had reported higher subjective value when controlling for the effect of reward outcome on choice (choice as a function of value difference: β = 0.92, z = 7.58, p<0.001; Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by logistic regression analysis of choice data.

claim: In the incidental memory version of Experiment 2, participants preferred images associated with higher rewards and higher subjective values, despite not being motivated to encode these associations.
source: Interestingly, both effects were replicated in the incidental memory version of the task, despite not motivating participants to encode nor associate images with their values and reward outcomes (choice as a function of reward difference: β = 1.21, z = 12.28, p<0.001; Figure 5C; choice as a function of value difference, controlling for reward difference: β = 1.03, z = 7.84, p<0.001; Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by logistic regression analysis of choice data.

claim: In all experiments, participants were more likely to prefer the outcome event the more positive the outcome RPE, and to prefer the cue event the more negative the outcome RPE.
source: In all experiments, we found that participants were more likely to prefer the outcome event the more positive the outcome RPE, and to prefer the cue event the more negative the outcome RPE (mixed-effects logistic regression, choice for outcome event as a function of signed outcome RPE, Experiment 1: β = 0.27, z = 3.27, p=0.001, Figure 6A; Experiment 2 - instructed memory: β = 0.23, z = 5.70, p<0.001, Figure 6B; Experiment 2 - incidental memory: β = 0.16, z = 4.30, p<0.001, Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by logistic regression analysis of choice data across all experiments.

claim: The preference effect of signed outcome RPE held when controlling for the magnitude of the outcome RPE.
source: Moreover, each one of these effects held when controlling for the magnitude of the outcome RPE, that is the unsigned outcome RPE (which boosted memory for outcome images, see 'Unsigned but not signed reward prediction errors at outcome enhanced memory', above), thus suggesting this preference may not be driven by better memory for large RPE events.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis controlling for confounding variables.

claim: Unsigned RPEs at reward outcome modulated trial-specific learning rate, consistent with a Pearce-Hall model of learning.
source: Drawing on classic associative models of attention (Pearce and Mackintosh, 2010), we found that an unsigned RPE at reward outcome modulated trial-specific learning rate, consistent with a Pearce-Hall model of learning that assumes more attention – and therefore more learning – for cues associated with unpredictable outcomes (Pearce and Hall, 1980).
evidence: Supported by computational modeling results and citation to the Pearce-Hall model.

claim: A signed RPE at reward cue modulated learning rate, consistent with a Mackintosh model of learning.
source: Similarly, a signed RPE at reward cue also modulated learning rate, consistent with a Mackintosh, 1975 model of learning that assumes enhanced attention to reward-predicting cues.
evidence: Supported by computational modeling results and citation to the Mackintosh model.

claim: Reinforcement learning models that included both Pearce-Hall and Mackintosh modulatory components predicted behavior better than models without those attentional components.
source: Reinforcement learning models that included both modulatory components predicted behavior better than models without those attentional components.
evidence: Supported by model comparison results.

claim: Unsigned RPEs at reward outcome improved memory for trial-unique scenes accompanying both the cue and outcome, most prominently the latter, in Experiment 1.
source: We found that unsigned RPEs at reward outcome improved memory for trial-unique scenes accompanying both the cue and outcome, most prominently the latter.
evidence: Supported by memory analysis results from Experiment 1.

claim: Memory for the cue event increased with learning in Experiment 2.
source: Unlike Experiment 1, where memory for the cue event remained relatively stable throughout the task, in Experiment 2, memory for the cue event (but not for the outcome event) increased with learning.
evidence: Supported by memory analysis results comparing Experiments 1 and 2.

claim: The mnemonic increase for cue events in Experiment 2 was supported by the gradual buildup of a signed RPE at cue.
source: This mnemonic increase for cue events was supported by the gradual buildup of a signed RPE at cue, which enhanced memory for more valued reward cues, as well as an unsigned RPE at cue that benefited memory the more participants had separated the values of the two reward categories (i.e. the more they had learned).
evidence: Supported by memory analysis results showing effects of both signed and unsigned cue RPEs.

claim: Individual learning performance predicted the increase in cue memory over learning.
source: Furthermore, we found that individual learning performance predicted the increase in cue memory over learning, providing another link between stronger reward expectations and enhanced memory for cue events.
evidence: Supported by individual differences analysis.

claim: The mnemonic benefits of RPEs are not a result of strategic encoding.
source: Importantly, our results were similar in both versions of Experiment 2, one that instructed memory for the images and their values and one where memory was completely incidental, confirming that the mnemonic benefits of RPEs are not a result of strategic encoding.
evidence: Supported by comparison of results between instructed and incidental memory conditions.

claim: Higher signed RPEs at outcome led to 'irrational' preference for the outcome event when choosing between cue and outcome scenes of a single trial.
source: Additionally, when choosing between the cue and outcome scenes of a single trial (i.e. two scenes associated with the same reward and value), higher signed RPEs at outcome, which we did not find to modulate memory, nevertheless led to 'irrational' preference for the outcome event.
evidence: Supported by choice analysis results.

claim: Midbrain dopamine signals convey signed RPEs to target areas.
source: As mentioned, one dominant hypothesis is that dopaminergic midbrain signals convey signed RPEs to target areas (Barto, 1995; Montague et al., 1996; Schultz et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature on dopaminergic signaling.

claim: Unsigned RPEs increase noradrenergic and dopaminergic firing from the locus coeruleus.
source: Less well accepted, but also quite dominant is the idea that unsigned RPEs increase noradrenergic (as well as dopaminergic) firing from the LC (Takeuchi et al., 2016; Kempadoo et al., 2016; Wagatsuma et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on locus coeruleus function.

claim: Midbrain dopamine initiates 'behavioral activation' which promotes the integration of higher-order representations, giving rise to semantic memories.
source: Midbrain dopamine initiates 'behavioral activation' (Clewett and Murty, 2019), such as increased vigor during periods of reward anticipation (Niv et al., 2007), which is thought to promote the integration of higher-order representations, like value formation, giving rise to semantic memories (Duszkiewicz et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on dopamine and memory.

claim: The LC-norepinephrine system promotes selectivity for salient events such as surprising outcomes, giving rise to distinctive, episodic memories.
source: The LC-norepinephrine system, on the other hand, is thought to promote selectivity for salient events such as (positively or negatively) surprising outcomes, giving rise to distinctive, episodic memories (Duszkiewicz et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to literature on the LC-norepinephrine system and memory.

claim: Phasic signed RPEs at cue would initiate and enhance a sustained period of reward anticipation, leading to memory benefits for ensuing events.
source: However, based on our findings and the above mapping to neural substrates, we predict that phasic signed RPEs at cue would initiate and enhance a sustained (potentially ramping) period of reward anticipation, leading to memory benefits for ensuing events, regardless of their exact timepoint.
evidence: Based on speculation and inference from the current findings and literature.

claim: RPEs amplify anticipatory value according to a computational model by Iigaya and colleagues.
source: Iigaya and colleagues recently offered such a computational model whereby RPEs amplify anticipatory value (i.e. the 'pleasure of savoring'; Iigaya et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to computational modeling work.

claim: The hippocampus enhances the functional coupling between the dopaminergic midbrain and the ventromedial prefrontal cortex to boost reward anticipation.
source: They further suggested a neural circuit whereby the hippocampus – tracking unsigned RPEs at outcome – enhances the functional coupling between the dopaminergic midbrain (encoding the signed RPE at outcome) and the ventromedial prefrontal cortex (encoding anticipatory value) to boost reward anticipation.
evidence: Supported by citation to neural circuit model.

claim: More rewarding cues and more surprising outcomes were prioritized in memory, promoting adaptive behavior.
source: In our experiments, we found a collaborative interaction between reinforcement learning and episodic memory systems: more rewarding cues and more surprising outcomes were prioritized in memory, thereby promoting adaptive behavior.
evidence: Supported by the overall pattern of results from the experiments.

claim: Compromised feedback-based learning has been associated with enhanced episodic memory in other paradigms.
source: Nonetheless, in other paradigms, these two systems have been shown to compete for processing resources: compromised feedback-based learning has been associated with enhanced episodic memory, both behaviorally and neurally (Foerde et al., 2013; Wimmer et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature showing competition between learning and memory systems.

claim: Better memory for reward-predicting cues was associated with weaker striatal RPEs at reward outcome in a study by Wimmer et al.
source: In fact, Wimmer et al., 2014 showed that better memory for reward-predicting cues was associated with weaker striatal RPEs at reward outcome.
evidence: Supported by citation to specific study.

claim: Participants were paid 10% of the rewards they received on every trial regardless of their estimates in Experiment 1.
source: Participants were paid 10% of the rewards they received on every trial regardless of their estimates, in line with a Pavlovian conditioning environment.
evidence: Describes the experimental procedure.

claim: Participants were asked to make predictions to ensure they paid attention to outcomes in this passive-viewing, online task.
